quotes.text: You cannot change what you do not notice. Logging is just noticing, with a memory.
A number is not a judgement. It is information about what happened, and information helps.
Tracking is not about control. It is about clarity.
Most of us guess our portions wrong. A few weeks of honest logging fixes that for good.
What gets noticed gets better.
Awareness comes first. Improvement can wait a week or two.
Look at your day the way a good friend would: curious, not critical.
It takes ten seconds to log a meal and it teaches you something for weeks.
Once you know what a portion looks like, you cannot un-know it. That is the point.
You do not need to be precise. You need to be honest, and roughly right, most days.
A calorie is a unit of energy, nothing more. It is neither good nor bad. It is just what is on the plate.
The goal of tracking is not a perfect log. It is a clear picture.
Log the snack too. The ones nobody sees add up most quietly.
Numbers tell you what happened. You decide what it means.
Awareness is the cheapest diet there is, and the one that lasts.
When you see where the day’s energy came from, small changes become obvious.
Do not fear the number. Befriend it. It is only trying to help.
Use the data, not the drama.
A week of honest notes will teach you more than a month of good intentions.
Someone who knows their portions rarely needs to be told to eat more or less.
A snack is a small meal that did not tell anyone it was one.
Watching your intake is about being informed, not about being afraid of food.
Looking at what you ate is one of the quickest ways to discover what you actually like.
Weigh it, measure it, guess it, whichever you will keep doing. A rough log kept beats a perfect one abandoned.
Half of eating well is knowing what is in front of you.
Trends matter more than any single day. Zoom out before you judge.
One number is a moment. A week of numbers is a story.
Tracking is a mirror, not a report card.
The habit of paying attention is the real result. The numbers are just receipts.
When you are curious about your food, you are already changing how you eat.
Big changes often begin with a small surprise, such as learning how much is in that one cup of coffee.
Drinks count. So do the spoonfuls of oil, the extra chapati and the cup of chai with two sugars.
A day with a few gaps is better than a day with no notes at all.
The point of a log is not to be right about the past. It is to be a little wiser tomorrow.
Once you can see your day, you can shape your day.
Your plate holds more information than any diet book. Read it.
Log while it is fresh. Memory is a hopeful storyteller.
An honest log has no bad days, only useful ones.
Some days the log will look great and some days it will look real. Keep both.
The moment you start paying attention, the food starts to make sense.
Knowing is not the same as restricting. It is just the first step to choosing.
When the numbers surprise you, be curious. That is where you learn the most.
Look at the week, not the day. The week tells the truth.
Notice, do not nag. Your log is not your critic.
Be curious about your plate. It has been quietly telling you things for years.
